name: QRSAM (Quick Reaction Surface-to-Air Missile)

header.one_liner: DRDO-developed quick-reaction SAM for the Indian Army; range 25-30 km; can intercept fighters, helicopters, UAVs; based on Akash missile technology; in production.

what_it_is.prose: QRSAM (Quick Reaction Surface-to-Air Missile) is a DRDO-developed short-range air defence system designed for the Indian Army's Air Defence Corps. The system is based on the Akash missile technology but optimised for quick reaction against low-flying targets including fighters, helicopters, UAVs, and cruise missiles. The missile has a range of 25-30 km and an altitude ceiling of 10 km, with a dual-mode seeker combining Radio Frequency (RF) and Imaging Infrared (IIR) guidance. The system is vehicle-mounted on BEML Tatra 8x8 trucks and provides 360° coverage. Production is shared between BEL (radar, C4I) and BDL (missile assembly). QRSAM has been in operational service with the Indian Army since the early 2020s and has accumulated orders exceeding ₹4,000 crore. The system complements the longer-range Akash and Akash-NG SAMs in the Indian Army's layered air defence architecture.

faq.question: What is the difference between QRSAM and Akash?
faq.answer: QRSAM (Quick Reaction Surface-to-Air Missile) is a DRDO-developed short-range air defence system optimised for quick reaction against low-flying targets including fighters, helicopters, UAVs, and cruise missiles, with a range of 25-30 km and altitude ceiling of 10 km. Akash is a medium-range SAM with longer range (25-45 km for Mk-I, 80+ km for Akash-NG) and higher altitude ceiling (18 km). QRSAM uses a dual-mode RF+IIR seeker while Akash uses a passive seeker (Mk-I/Prime) or active radar seeker (NG). Both are produced by BEL (radar, C4I) and BDL (missile).

faq.question: Which Indian Army unit operates the QRSAM?
faq.answer: QRSAM is in operational service with the Indian Army's Air Defence Corps. The system is vehicle-mounted on BEML Tatra 8x8 trucks and provides 360° coverage for quick-reaction engagements against low-flying aerial threats. Specific regiment count and deployment locations have not been publicly disclosed. Aggregate orders across BEL and BDL exceed ₹4,000 crore.

faq.question: Why is QRSAM based on Akash missile technology?
faq.answer: QRSAM reuses the Akash missile's solid-propellant rocket motor and basic airframe design, but is packaged in a smaller, more agile configuration optimised for quick-reaction engagements. The dual-mode seeker (RF + IIR) provides robust end-game guidance against low-RCS targets like UAVs and cruise missiles that may defeat the Akash's passive seeker. This technology reuse allowed DRDO to field QRSAM quickly and at lower development cost than a clean-sheet design.
